{"body":"**Problem.** In the CUDA local warp, rounding in single precision can send a pixel on the last column or last row of the image to the nearest-pixel fallback where the CPU interpolates. This affects only a sliver of border pixels. Its incidence in real outputs has not been measured.

**Mechanism** (main `c8844894`). In `cuda_realspace_dw.cu` ([lines 146-191](https://github.com/KingAlejandro/MotionCorr-standalone/blob/c8844894/src/acc/cuda/cuda_realspace_dw.cu#L146-L191)), `x_target = (float)ix - x_fitted` is computed in float. Near x = 4095 one float step is 2.4e-4 px.
- For `ix = nx-1` and `0 < x_fitted < ~1.2e-4` px, `x_target` rounds to exactly `nx-1`. The check `x0 >= nx - 1` then marks the pixel invalid and takes `d_Iframe[y0*nx + x0]` for both axes.
- The CPU ([motioncorr_runner.cpp:4425-4475](https://github.com/KingAlejandro/MotionCorr-standalone/blob/c8844894/src/motioncorr_runner.cpp#L4425-L4475)) computes the same quantity in double, gets `x0 = nx-2`, and interpolates bilinearly.
- The same applies to `iy = ny-1`.
- Example from #256 §F: image `I[y,x] = y`, width 4096, x shift 1e-5 px and y shift 0.5 px. The CPU gives 0.5 at the last-column pixel; the CUDA float calculation gives 0.

The polynomial coefficients are also passed to the kernel as float, so `fx` and `fy` are only resolved to about 2.4e-4 px in the interior. That error is continuous and far smaller than the other CPU/CUDA differences; only the change of branch at the border is discrete.

**Scope.** The bug is specific to the CUDA port, and it applies only where the local motion model is used. The CPU's border policy, a nearest-pixel fallback whenever the target is outside `[0, n-1)`, is inherited and stays as it is. It is not related to S1, which is decided before the warp.

**Next action:**
1. Measure: on one S1-negative family (tutorial) and one 4096² family, count the last-row and last-column pixels where CPU and CUDA take different branches, given the same model coefficients.
2. Fix: compute `x_target`/`y_target`, or at least the branch decision, in double, or split the shift into integer and fractional parts before subtracting. Add a unit test with the example above that fails on the current kernel. Keep the border policy unchanged.

Source: #256 §F; earlier exploration in #232.
","comments":[{"id":"IC_kwDOUnH-pc8AAAABd8lCDg","author":{"login":"KingAlejandro"},"authorAssociation":"OWNER","body":"## Tighten the boundary and measurement scope

The source-level branch issue is real, and retaining the current border policy in the first repair is sensible. Two qualifications will make the native test more useful:

1. Count disagreements near the **source-coordinate boundary**, not only at the output image's last row/column. In the production kernel `x_target = ix - x_fitted`; a fitted displacement can move an interior output pixel arbitrarily close to `nx-1` (or the other bounds). For example, the same cancellation witness can be moved several output columns inward by adding an integer part to the displacement. Scan the full output or explicitly select pixels whose unrounded source coordinates lie near each branch boundary. Include last-row, last-column, corner, inward/outward and interior-output/edge-source controls.
2. Separate **coordinate subtraction** from **motion-field evaluation**. Using double only for `ix - x_fitted` prevents one cancellation mechanism, but cannot recover information already lost when polynomial coefficients or `x_fitted` were rounded to float. First give CPU/GPU identical per-pixel displacements, then compare the actual production kernels with identical full-precision model coefficients. Report both branch disagreement and pixel-value error, and show which narrowing conversion the chosen repair addresses.

The fallback is for both axes: an x-boundary decision can discard otherwise valid y interpolation. Use a y ramp to make that loss visible and repeat with x/y exchanged; constant images are a negative control. Include a mutant that restores only the float coordinate operation, and invoke the actual production kernel in Release rather than a separately reimplemented test body.

Scope wording: this cannot initiate upstream **trajectory/patch-acceptance divergence**, because warping happens later. However S1 is also reported using **final-image relative RMSE**, so “not related to S1” is too absolute. Its contribution to that output metric remains unmeasured. Whole-image, interior and edge-band errors under a fixed model will bound that contribution without confusing it with estimator feedback.
